opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a single moment. It was a slow, kind of painful realization over maybe a year or so.

Taichi started as my PhD project at MIT. It was something I really loved: a programming language that made high-performance parallel computing, especially for physical simulation and graphics, much more accessible. The open-source community grew really fast, lots of GitHub stars, lots of users in academia and industry. So when we started the company, the natural assumption was that Taichi itself would be the business.

But over time, we had to face a hard truth: a programming language, especially an open-source one, is a really difficult thing to monetize. People love using it, but that doesn't mean they'll pay for it. We tried different directions, enterprise support, tooling, building things on top of it, and the numbers just weren't adding up the way a company needs them to. Meanwhile, I was responsible for a team, for investors' money, for people who left good jobs to join us.

The hardest part was emotional. Taichi felt like my child. Admitting it couldn't carry the company felt, at first, like admitting failure. What helped me was reframing it: Taichi wasn't a failure. It gave us a world-class team, deep expertise in graphics and compute, and credibility. It was the foundation, just not the product.

Then generative AI started taking off, and we saw that 3D content creation was a huge pain point, and our team was uniquely positioned to tackle it. That's how Meshy came about. Once I saw a direction where users were genuinely eager to pay because it solved a real problem for them, letting go of Taichi as the core business became much easier. You stop asking "how do I save the thing I built?" and start asking "what's the most valuable thing this team can build next?"

So I'd say acceptance came from being honest with the data, and from realizing that being loyal to your mission matters more than being loyal to a specific project.

r001.rationale: The response says Taichi was hard to monetize and could not carry the company, but it does not mention Hu’s desire to prove himself through commercializing it.

r002.rationale: The response describes giving up Taichi as emotionally painful, but does not compare it to effectively firing himself.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a single moment. It was more like a slow admission that I kept postponing.

Taichi started as my PhD project at MIT. It was something I genuinely loved building: a programming language for high-performance graphics and physical simulation, and the open-source community around it grew faster than I ever expected. Tens of thousands of stars on GitHub, people in universities, studios, research labs all over the world using it. When we raised money and started the company, the natural assumption was that this thing everyone loves must become a business.

But the gap between "people love this" and "people will pay for this" turned out to be enormous. The users who got the most value from Taichi were researchers and individual developers, and they were never going to be a revenue base. The enterprises that could pay didn't want a language. They wanted a product that solved a concrete problem, and a general-purpose compiler is a long way from that. We tried different directions, simulation tooling, developer services, and each one taught us something, but none of them produced the kind of pull where customers are chasing you rather than the other way around.

What made it hard emotionally is that Taichi was tied to my identity. For years I was "the Taichi guy." Stepping back from it felt like admitting I had been wrong, and I had a lot of people in the community who trusted that we would keep pushing it forward. So I kept telling myself one more quarter, one more experiment.

The thing that eventually shifted was separating two questions I had been mixing up. One is "is Taichi valuable?" and the answer is clearly yes. The other is "is Taichi the right foundation for this company to survive and grow?" and the honest answer was no. Once I let those two be different questions, it stopped feeling like a betrayal. The open-source project can keep existing and keep being useful without the company's survival being staked on it.

And then there was the practical side. We had a team of very talented people, a runway that was not infinite, and the broader shift happening in AI was opening up problems that our skills, compilers, GPU programming, performance engineering, were genuinely well suited for. At some point, being a responsible founder meant choosing the direction where the company could actually win, rather than the direction that made me feel most comfortable.

I still think of it as one of the harder decisions I've made. Not because it was intellectually difficult. In hindsight the signals were all there. It was hard because I had to let go of a story about myself. But I'd rather build a company that lasts than protect a narrative.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Taichi was tied to Hu’s identity and that he kept postponing the decision, but it does not identify a desire to prove himself through commercialization. It says he concluded Taichi was not the right foundation for the company, without describing that specific conflict.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes stepping back from Taichi as feeling like admitting he was wrong and letting go of a story about himself. It does not convey that he regarded the decision as effectively firing himself.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficult part is separating two questions: Is Taichi valuable technology? And can it support a company as its core business? Those aren’t the same question. You can care deeply about a project and still need a clearer answer about who will pay for it and what problem you’re solving for them.

As a founder, you have to be willing to revisit your original assumption. The technology can remain valuable, but the company needs to be organized around a customer need. Accepting that means letting go of the idea that the thing you started with must always be the center of the business.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes Taichi’s value from its viability as a core business, but does not mention Hu’s desire to prove himself through commercialization or his inability to see a commercial future for it.

r002.rationale: The response does not convey that giving up Taichi as the company’s core business felt like firing himself.

sol-6.1.text:
It was a gradual realization. Taichi was something I cared about deeply, so it was hard to separate my attachment to the technology from the question of whether it could sustain a company. Those are two different things.

You can build something technically interesting that people enjoy using, but a business also needs a problem customers urgently want solved and are willing to pay for. Eventually, I had to ask: are we following that demand, or are we trying to find a business that lets us keep working on our favorite technology?

Accepting that distinction made it easier to move forward. Taichi could still be valuable without being the company’s core business.

r001.rationale: The response says Hu had to distinguish his attachment to Taichi from its commercial viability, but it does not convey a desire to prove himself through commercialization or that he could not see a future for Taichi as the company’s core business.

r002.rationale: The response describes accepting that Taichi need not remain the core business, but does not compare that decision to firing himself.
